food.text: Norse settlements on Greenland's western coast peaked at 2,000 to 3,000 people. They were sustained by pastoral farming and by exports to Europe, mainly of walrus ivory.

Between AD 800 and 1300, the fjord regions of southern Greenland were several degrees Celsius warmer than usual for the North Atlantic. Trees and herbaceous plants grew, livestock was farmed, and barley was grown as a crop up to the 70th parallel.

Bone samples from Greenland Norse cemeteries show that by the mid-14th century the typical Greenlander's diet had shifted from 20 percent sea animals to 80 percent. As the climate cooled, people who had arrived as farmers were living more and more off the sea.

Norse settlements on Greenland's western coast peaked at a population of 2,000 to 3,000. They were sustained by pastoral farming on scattered coastal fjords and by exports, mainly of walrus ivory, to Europe.

As the Little Ice Age set in, middens on Norse farms show a shift from the bones of cows and pigs to those of sheep and goats. Bone samples from Norse cemeteries show the typical diet rose from 20 percent sea animals to 80 percent.

Excavations of middens on Norse farms in Greenland and Iceland show a shift from the bones of cows and pigs to those of sheep and goats. The trend followed the cooling climate, which left less time each year to grow hay.

The Greenland settlements traded walrus tusk ivory with Europe, and, according to one 13th-century account, also exported rope, sheep, seals, wool and cattle hides. All of this trade passed exclusively through Bergen and Trondheim.

The Dorset people were highly adapted to the cold, and much of their food is thought to have come from hunting sea mammals that breathe through holes in the ice. The sea-ice decline caused by the Medieval Warm Period would have strongly affected them.

As winters lengthened and springs and summers shortened after about 1300, Greenlanders had less and less time to grow hay. By 1420 the Little Ice Age had reached intense levels in Greenland, squeezing the fodder supply that kept their livestock alive.
By the mid-14th century, deposits from a chieftain's farm held a large number of cattle and caribou remains. A poorer farm only a few kilometres away had no trace of domestic animals, only seal.

According to one 13th-century account, the Greenland settlements exported rope, sheep, seals, wool and cattle hides, alongside walrus ivory. Trade with Greenland took place exclusively through Bergen and Trondheim.

Around 1350 the church in Norse Greenland owned the largest farm and around two thirds of the best pasture land. Significant benefices were set up to support the bishops who followed the first, Arnaldr.

Around 700 BCE, Norton inhabitants of St. Lawrence Island and other Bering Strait islands developed an even more specialized way of life based entirely on the ocean. This shift toward marine food sources became known as the Thule tradition.

art.text: Around 1000 CE, the Thule people replaced the Dorset in the Canadian Arctic. The Dorset had carved walrus ivory mainly for ceremonial use, while the art of the Thule was more decorative in character.

art.text: Christian churches and chapels have been excavated on numerous Norse farms in Greenland. The Church of Brattahlíð fits exactly the account of the little church of Thjodhild in the Grœnlendinga saga.
Greenland's Norse churches were built by the landlord of each farm. Because he built the church, he was also initially entitled to the taxes payable by the parish.

The Dorset culture left distinctive artifacts, including triangular end-blades and oil lamps called qulliq made of soapstone. The culture lasted until sometime between 1000 CE and 1500 CE, and the Thule people replaced it.

war.text: Erik the Red's Greenland colony, which grew to 5,000 inhabitants, was ravaged in 1002 when a group of immigrants brought an epidemic that killed many of its leading citizens, including Erik himself. The colony rebounded and survived until the Little Ice Age made the land marginal for European life-styles in the 15th century. Pirate raids, conflict with Inuit moving into the Norse territories, and the colony's abandonment by Norway became other factors in its decline.

According to Greenlandic Inuit oral tradition, Inuit warriors under K'aissape approached the Norse settlement of Hvalsey by sea disguised as an iceberg. They then burned the Norse settlers to death inside their houses. It was revenge for the slaying of K'aissape's younger brother by the Norse chieftain Ungortoq, and Ungortoq escaped with his family.

Both Inuit and Norse oral traditions preserved accounts of contact and conflict between the two peoples in Greenland, republished by scholar Gwyn Jones in The Norse Atlantic Sagas. Jones noted that the Norse version of the story was of more doubtful provenance than the Inuit account.

In the same Inuit legend, chieftain Ungortoq escaped the burning of Hvalsey with his family, but the warrior K'aissape hunted him down and slew him and his whole family near Cape Farewell. This ended the blood feud that began when Ungortoq slew K'aissape's younger brother.

An Inuit account tells of a kayaker who sent his spear out in good earnest and killed a Norseman on the spot. When winter came, it was a general belief that the Kavdlunait, the Inuit word for foreigners or Europeans, would come and avenge the death of their countrymen.

Despite the vivid Inuit legend that Hvalsey was burned down, archaeological studies of the site have found no sign of a fire. Historians instead point to causes such as soil erosion from overgrazing and the Black Death to explain the end of the Norse settlement there.

literature.text: The Saga of Erik the Red and the Saga of the Greenlanders, both thought to have been written around 1200, tell of the voyages to Vinland. They are generally regarded as works of literature rather than purely historical accounts, and scholars debate their factual accuracy.

Greenlandic Norse is an extinct North Germanic language spoken in the Norse settlements of Greenland until their demise in the late 15th century. It is known mainly from runic inscriptions found in Greenland, which show innovations such as the use of initial t for þ.

The Kingittorsuaq Runestone has one of the longest Norse inscriptions found in Greenland. It was discovered near Upernavik, far north of the Norse settlements, and was presumably carved by Norse explorers. Like most Greenlandic inscriptions it is traditionally dated to c. 1300.

A marriage certificate written at Garðar in Greenland in 1409 survives in an Icelandic transcription from 1625, attested by bishop Oddur Einarsson. Two Greenland-based priests attested the banns for two Icelanders blown off course to Greenland, Þorsteinn Ólafsson and Sigríður Björnsdóttir.

The 1409 Greenland document is clearly not in Icelandic and cannot without reservation be called Norwegian. It uses the form þil for the older til, showing the merger of initial þ and t, which matches the evidence of the runic inscriptions.

The poem Atlamál is credited as Greenlandic in the Codex Regius. However, the preserved text reflects Icelandic scribal conventions, so it is not certain that the poem was actually composed in Greenland.

The most important written source on Greenland from the 14th century is the description by Ívarr Bárðarson, who stayed there for several years. The Skarðárannáll by Björn Jónsson á Skarðsá also enjoys a high reputation, though some dating errors appear in later additions.

Icelandic chronicles record that in 1121 bishop Eric Gnupsson, who had been based on Greenland since 1112, went to seek Vinland. Nothing more is reported of him. No written records other than inscribed stones survive from Greenland, so later voyages, such as a ship blown off course in 1347 while returning from Markland with timber, are known from Icelandic chronicles.

Marie Stoklund has called for reconsideration of the dating of the Greenlandic runic material. She points out that some parallels to the Kingittorsuaq inscription elsewhere in the Nordic world have been dated to c. 1200, rather than c. 1300.

science.text: Vinland was known only from the sagas and medieval historiography until 1960. That year Helge Ingstad and Anne Stine Ingstad found the remains of Norse buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland, which further proved Norse exploration of mainland North America.

The Thule culture migrated eastward from what is now Alaska around 1000 AD and reached Greenland around 1300. It was the first to introduce technological innovations such as dog sleds and toggling harpoons to Greenland.

A study of North Atlantic seasonal temperature variability found that maximum summer temperatures fell significantly from the late 13th century to early 14th century, by as much as 6 to 8 °C compared with modern summers. The lowest winter temperatures of the last 2000 years came in the late 14th and early 15th centuries. The Western Settlement's demise coincides with this cooling.

Norse settlements on Greenland's western coast peaked at 2,000 to 3,000 people, sustained by pastoral farming and exports of walrus ivory to Europe. For timber and iron, the colonists launched expeditions into the Canadian Arctic and likely into the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

The Dorset culture is defined as having four phases because of distinct differences in hunting and tool-making technologies. Its artifacts include distinctive triangular end-blades, oil lamps called qulliq made of soapstone, and burins.

In the 1420s, Scandinavian accounts such as the work of Claudius Clavus depicted Greenland as a peninsula joined to northern Russia. Arctic sea ice may have made this description true for practical purposes. Greenland is not known to have been successfully circumnavigated until the 20th century.

Archaeoentomologists dated domestic insects found in the permafrost around GUS, and these insects died out when the Norse abandoned the colony. Their diet showed the conditions at the end: after a very poor growing season, the final colonists began eating their dogs and livestock, and were likely near starvation during the winter. The last farms were likely abandoned around 1360 AD.

Excavations of middens from Norse farms in Greenland and Iceland show a shift from the bones of cows and pigs to those of sheep and goats. As winters lengthened and springs and summers shortened, Greenlanders had less and less time to grow hay.

Bone samples from Greenland Norse cemeteries confirm that by the mid-14th century the typical Greenlander diet had increased from 20 percent sea animals to 80 percent. This shift accompanied the cooling climate of the Little Ice Age.

A genetic study published in Science in August 2014 examined nineteen Dorset people buried in Canada and Greenland up to 1320 CE. It found the Dorset were genetically distinct from the Thule, who replaced them around 1300 CE. It also found no evidence of genetic mixing with the Greenlandic Norse.

From 1402 to 1404 the Black Death hit Iceland for the first time and killed approximately half its population. Because trade with Greenland ran through Bergen and Trondheim, Ludvig Holberg concluded the plague also reached Greenland. A mass grave near Narsarsuaq is unclear evidence, since the conditions for plague to spread were probably lacking.

From 1991 to 1996, the Danish Polar Center and the University of Alberta studied a farm called "Gården under sandet" (Farm beneath the sand) in Greenland's Western Settlement, dating to between 1000 and 1400. The excavation gave insights into how Viking residential buildings were built and how the residents got their food.

Radiocarbon dating has shown the Dorset were living in the Cambridge Bay area as late as 1350 CE, while the Thule Inuit moved into the area around 1200 CE. The dates suggest the two peoples overlapped in the region, though it is not fully known whether they ever met.

Radiocarbon dating helps show how long Greenland's Norse settlements lasted. Archaeologists found evidence of one house in use potentially as late as 1409. As of 2002, the most recent radiocarbon date found in Norse settlements was 1430, give or take 15 years.

politics.text: Greenland was politically and culturally associated with the European kingdom of Norway from 986 until the early 15th century. In 1380 Norway entered a personal union with Denmark, and from 1397 it was part of the Kalmar Union.

Norse Greenland was organised into three settlements on fjords near the island's southwestern tip. Settlers led by Erik the Red arrived in a contingent of 14 boats, and they formed the Eastern Settlement, the Western Settlement and the Middle Settlement.

Greenland's Norse settlers requested a bishop in 1126 and in 1261 accepted the overlordship of the Norwegian king. They kept their own law and became almost completely politically independent after 1349, the time of the Black Death. In 1380, Norway entered a personal union with Denmark.

Denmark-Norway inherited the medieval Norwegian claim to Greenland when the Kalmar Union was ratified in 1397. The claim outlived the Norse settlement itself, which had disappeared by the 15th century, and Europeans did not settle the island again until 1721.
Medieval Greenland was a bishopric with 22 churches and 2 convents under the archdiocese of Nidaros. In 1261 the Greenlanders became subjects of the Kingdom of Norway.

The Grœnlendinga saga reports that in 1118 the Greenland colony sent Einarr Sokkason to Norway to persuade King Sigurðr Jórsalafari to give Greenland its own bishop. The first Greenlandic bishop was Arnaldr from 1126. Until the 11th century, Greenland had been under the Archdiocese of Bremen.

In 1261 the Norse settlers in Greenland accepted the overlordship of the Norwegian king, though they kept their own law. They became almost completely politically independent after 1349, the time of the Black Death. In 1380 the Kingdom of Norway entered into a personal union with the Kingdom of Denmark.

Around 1350 the Greenland church owned the largest farm and about two thirds of the best pasture land. Significant benefices were set up to support the bishops who followed the first Greenlandic bishop, Arnaldr, who took office in 1126.

Church power in Greenland grew large. Around 1350 the church owned the largest farm and around two thirds of the best pasture land. Churches were built by the landlord, who was initially entitled to the taxes payable by the parish.

A union between Norway and Sweden, including Greenland and Iceland, existed between 1319 and 1355 through Magnus IV of Sweden, who was crowned Magnus VII in Norway. It returned between 1362 and 1364 through his son Haakon VI.
The last bishop at Garðar died in 1377. After a marriage recorded in 1408, no written records mention the Norse settlers of Greenland.

philosophy.text: Traditional Inuit religious belief held that every person had two souls, one of which could leave the body at night. Separately, ghosts and spirits were believed to sometimes visit a person through their dreams.

Inuit communities relied on angakkuit, spiritual mediators who during training gained a helper spirit called a tuurngaq, visible only to them. Inuit stories tell of angakkuit who, with a tuurngaq's help, could run as fast as caribou or even fly. In some traditions an angakkuq was stabbed or shot to prove his power, and the intervention of his tuurngaq meant he received no wound.

Inughuit of northern Greenland and Labrador Inuit both held a recurring belief that ghosts and spirits could visit a person through their dreams. This idea reflected the wider Inuit view that dreams carried real spiritual significance.

Angakkuit of the Central Inuit held an annual ceremony to appease the Sea Woman Sedna, who became angry when her taboos were broken and who lacks fingers. The angakkuq travelled in spirit to her underworld home, Adlivun, and smoothed out her hair. He then begged or fought with Sedna to make sure his people would not starve, and Inuit believed his pleading and apologies would let the animals return and hunters succeed.
West Greenlandic legend held that angakkut who traveled to the spirit world in soul form faced real danger. They were said to be repeatedly almost captured by the fearsome spirit Amarsiniook.

culture.text: The Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and spread eastward across northern Canada, reaching Greenland by the 13th century. In the process they replaced the earlier Dorset culture who had lived in the region.

The Thule brought technological advances to Greenland, including dog sleds and toggling harpoons. These were the first such innovations introduced there, and they helped the Thule thrive in the Arctic environment.

The Norse settlers in Greenland built Christian churches and chapels on numerous farms, including the Church of Brattahlíð. The Grœnlendinga saga's account of the little church of Thjodhild fits it exactly, and the landlord who built each church was also entitled to the parish taxes.

In the early 12th century, Greenland's Norse colonists sought their own bishop, and in 1126 Arnaldur arrived as the first bishop of Garðar. He began building Garðar Cathedral, dedicated to St Nicholas, patron saint of sailors, which became the first Catholic diocese in the Americas.

Inuit legends recount meeting people they called the Tuniit, who are linked to the Dorset, though whether the two peoples really met is uncertain. According to legend, these first inhabitants were giants, taller and stronger than the Inuit, but afraid to interact and "easily put to flight". Other Inuit oral history describes the Tuniit as gentle and shy, without bows or arrows, and says they were easily killed or driven away.

The diocese of Garðar first answered to the Archdiocese of Bremen, then to Lund from 1126. In 1152 it became a suffragan of the newly created Norwegian Archdiocese of Nidaros, alongside the dioceses of Iceland, the Isle of Man, Orkney and the Faroe Islands.

From 1341, Norwegian clergyman Ívar Bárðarson served as the Catholic Church's official representative in Greenland. He filled the vacant bishopric at Garðar Cathedral until a new bishop could be ordained.

The Dorset made oil lamps called qulliq from soapstone, and much of their food is thought to have come from hunting sea mammals that breathe through holes in the ice. Their culture is named after Cape Dorset, now Kinngait, in Nunavut.
The Greenland Norse traded with Europe in ivory from walrus tusks. According to one 13th-century account, they also exported rope, sheep, seals, wool and cattle hides.

Before burial, Inuit women washed the body of the dead, then wrapped it in a large blanket of caribou hide or wool and laid it face up far out on the tundra, with cairns stacked on top to keep scavengers off. The cairns did not always work: scattered human bones can still be found across the tundra, testifying to the work of carnivores. Qilakitsoq mummies dating from 500 years ago show that the Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, wrapped and protected their dead in the same way.

Garðar's third bishop, Jón Árnason, nicknamed Smyril, took office in 1189. Between 1202 and 1203 he made a pilgrimage to Rome and met Pope Innocent III, then died at Garðar in 1209, likely buried in the cathedral's Northern Chapel.
By around 1350 the Christian church in Greenland's Norse colony owned the largest farm in the settlement. It also held roughly two thirds of the best pasture land.

Some Greenland Norse who were willing to adopt Inuit ways and means may have intermarried with the Inuit. Yet a 2015 genetic study of modern-day Greenlanders found no evidence of Norse ancestry among them, despite earlier speculation.
In 1343 Norway ordained Jón Skalli as a new bishop of Garðar after wrongly assuming Bishop Árni had died. When Árni turned out to be alive, Skalli resigned and never traveled to Greenland.
